answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text: Consequential accounting (which is different from "marginal impact") is a promising tool to help decarbonize the power sector in combination with other approaches. It can help direct investment to emissions hotspots around the globe and provide insight into decisionmaking on how we interact with and use the grid. If grounded in the well-established science of lifecycle assessment, it can provide a complementary perspective to Scope 2 accounting. However, it also comes with substantial risks that should not be brushed aside. Ignoring the "consequential" foundation of this science and instead focusing on just its "marginal" aspects, or just treating this approach as a feasibility release valve for more complex and robust Scope 2 accounting opens the door to greenwashing and erodes its impact. Consequential accounting, when done right, is quite complex and nuanced, and in many ways may be as equally if not more challenging to implement as the proposed scope 2 changes: it requires temporally and locationally granular accounting of activity and emissions factors, it requires strict quality criteria, and consideration of nuanced interactions with local policy and market environments. The current lack of standardized or verifiable emissions factors may make comparability, verification, and credibility difficult. Without strict guiderails, it has the potential to lead to widespread greenwashing and deviate from its theoretical promise to accelerate grid decarbonization. I am excited by the potential of consequential accounting, but it is equally important to consider and manage its risks so that it lives up to its potential.

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text: If the goal is just to quantify impact from a generation project, then this formula is appropriate in that it considers both hour-specific and location-specific emission factors and activity data, which is critical for accurate calculation, since marginal impacts vary both in time and space. However, this formula is secondary to the initial determination of whether there is any consequential impact at all, which depends on factors such as additionality and interaction with other policy environments such as cap-and-trade systems or RPS. This formula also ignores impact of demand side actions on the grid.

answers.label: Secondary effects to consider, and how
answers.text: If the goal is to quantify and minimize "global emissions impact", then consideration of all secondary effects would be appropriate, not only including upstream and downstream Scope 3 emissions, but also any secondary grid impacts beyond the marginal generators (which may or may not be included in the MER).

answers.label: Why secondary effects should be excluded
answers.text: If the goal is to just provide a first order approximation or incentive signal, and not account for global atmospheric emission changes, then including secondary effects may not be necessary. However, some proximate lifecycle information may still be relevant (eg fugitive methane emissions for natural gas, which in some cases makes natural gas generation more GHG intensive than coal, which would affect decision and investment outcomes).

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text: Forward-looking projections of emissions impacts have low certainty of both the activity data and the MERs, and it would likely be inappropriate to quantify any impacts upfront.

answers.label: Additionality tests missing from the framework
answers.text:
I would also recommend a set of "permanence tests" which evaluate whether the emissions impacts would be permanent or subject to conditions that cause emissions rebound.

Example 1: Cap and trade region. As explained by the Clean Energy Buyer's Institute: "When a project activity is located in a region with a cap-and-trade program, such as the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, California’s Cap and Trade Program, and the European Union Emissions Trading System, there is a risk that the indirect emissions reductions at the marginal generator caused by the activity may allow for increased emissions at other times or at other generators, resulting in no net emissions reductions in the long term. In cap-and-trade programs, a regulatory cap is set on total emissions, and emitters must buy and trade emissions allowances to cover all their emissions. When the emissions cap is binding, taking an action that reduces power sector emissions may free up emissions allowances that can be used to pollute at a later time or be sold to another emitter that allows them to emit more. This risk can be mitigated by purchasing and retiring cap-and-trade allowances equivalent to the estimated emissions impact of a decision or reporting the activity as a voluntary set-aside in the cap-andtrade program (if such set-asides exist)."

Example 2: REC Swapping in RPS regions (also from CEBI): "Another risk to the long-term avoided emissions impact of a new clean energy project occurs when an energy customer engages in renewable energy certificate (REC) swapping or REC arbitrage. When procuring clean energy located in a state with a renewable portfolio standard (RPS), the price of these “compliance-grade” RECs may be higher than RECs from voluntary markets because there are differences in eligible supply that can qualify for each market. Thus, some energy customers will sell their project’s RECs for use in the local RPS and buy cheaper RECs from other (often existing) sources, arbitraging the value between the two types of
RECs. However, if the RECs that were sold away are now used to help meet compliance with the RPS targets, this reduces the amount of clean
energy that the local utility would have otherwise been mandated to procure. Engaging in this type of REC swap means that the voluntary clean
energy procurement is no longer incremental to the amount of clean energy procurement that was mandated to happen anyway. To reduce this
risk, energy customers would want to ensure that any compliance-grade RECs they sell are ultimately retired in a voluntary market, or avoid REC swapping altogether.

answers.label: Details on operating margin methodologies
answers.text:
Implied heat rate approaches lack robustness. The assumptions of this model break down if multiple fuel types can be on the margin (which is true in most regions) or if generator dispatch deviates from what heat rates would suggest. Additionally, WattTime, who implements the the SGIP Signal in California, has previously explored using this approach across all grid regions in the U.S. and found that it performed poorly in predicting real-world generator behavior.
Difference based models lack any semblance of causal linkage and are not necessarily reasonable approximations of consequential impact.
For a comprehensive discussion of the plusses and minuses of these methods see: 1) https://cebi.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/Guide-to-Sourcing-Marginal-Emissions-Factor-Data.pdf and 2) https://www.watttime.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/WattTime-MOER-modeling-20221004.pdf

answers.label: Details on build margin methodologies
answers.text:
Build margin signals are less studied than operating margin signals, but all of these could be reasonable approximations.
One major limitation of recent capacity additions is that it only predicts generator additions (in response to increased load) but not retirements (ie in response to new generation).
The most controversial on this list may be "average emissions rates" because for a long time the marginal emissions literature found that these were not appropriate for operational MERS. However, emerging research (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5985015) finds that average emission rates actually perform quite well in long-run marginal emissions impact, so (granular, location-based) average emissions rates may be reasonable here.

answers.label: Assessing model applicability to project types
answers.text: True consequential impacts (ie including all interactive and secondary effects) can be affected by the size of a project, its predictability, and how it is planned for. This is because individual projects have different consequential impacts on different operational grid timescales (see pages 11-18 here: https://cebi.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/Applying-The-Consequential-Emissions-Framework-For-Emissions-Optimized-Decision-Making-For-Energy-Procurement-And-Management.pdf)

answers.label: Other appropriate emission rates or metrics
answers.text: If the goal is to incentivize action rather than accurately quantify consequential emissions impacts, then other signals such as clean energy curtailment volumes, clean energy fractions, or wholesale market prices may also perform well. See: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5985015.

answers.label: Why that spatial granularity ceiling
answers.text: If by "maximum" you mean "largest" then BA level is the largest that should be used. In general, the more granular the better due to locational impacts on the grid. So only BA, Zonal, or Nodal should be used.

answers.label: Why that temporal granularity ceiling
answers.text: If by "maximum" you mean "least granular" then hourly. So only hourly or sub-hourly rates should be used. This is because marginal emissions impacts are highly temporally variable.

Research supporting the suggested approach
answers.text:
https://cebi.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/Applying-The-Consequential-Emissions-Framework-For-Emissions-Optimized-Decision-Making-For-Energy-Procurement-And-Management.pdf (pages 17-18)

Metrics such as net qualifying capacity (NQC) and effective load carrying capacity (ELCC) have been used commonly to establish how well a resource contributes to reliability needs during peak hours. Since peak hours tend to drive capacity expansion needs, these factors could be a reasonable approximation of a build margin weight.

An NQC/ELCC-like approach could potentially be used to establish build margin weights for each resource

CAISO splits these factors by geography and month of the year to reflect temporal and spatially-varying values of capacity. These values are typically calculated per season/month, region, and resource technology.

CAISO uses a specific (publicly documented) modeling approach to determine these factors, although similar factors could be potentially calculated using a simpler method (eg average capacity factor in the peak hour window for each grid region.

One feature of pure ELCC calculations is that they reflect “diminishing returns’: the more of a resource that is built, the more it meets system peak needs and pushes the peak to another time period that may be not as well served by that resource. This means that over time, the build margin weight of an oversaturated resource would decrease, putting more of an emphasis on the operating margin.

Another feature of an ELCC value is that if a storage project is operated economically, and prices are correlated with peak times, the storage device may have an ELCC near 100%, meaning that storage would primarily affect the build margin rather than the operating margin, although over time, that may decrease.

ELCC values have been widely used/explored by many of the major grid operators in the U.S., so ELCC values may already be publicly available in many regions. See: https://blog.ucs.org/mark-specht/to-understand-energy-storage-you-must-understand-elcc/, https://blog.ucs.org/mark-specht/elcc-explained-the-critical-renewable-energy-concept-youve-never-heard-of/, https://www.utilitydive.com/news/adding-it-all-up-counting-the-capacity-contribution-of-variable-and-durati/584843/#:~:text=Both%20California%20and%20Midwest%20Independent,and%20procuring%20non%2Dfirm%20resources
